<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> <b><i><u><font size="2" face="Arial">We may experience cost pressure as our labor force becomes more senior, and if attrition
increases, we may not be able to replace our current workforce with candidates that meet our high recruiting and training standards.</font></u></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></b> Labor costs, including medical and workers compensation costs, constitute a significant percentage of our total operating costs, and wage rates, in
general, are increasing due to cost of living adjustments within our collective bargaining agreements.&nbsp;&nbsp;In an effort to&nbsp;return to profitability, we reduced our work force significantly and obtained wage and salary concessions from each of our employee
groups.&nbsp;&nbsp;As a result, our employees may elect to seek other employment opportunities, thereby increasing our recruiting and training costs.&nbsp; We cannot guarantee that we will be able to continue to find qualified personnel to fill&nbsp;any vacancies
that may arise in the future.&nbsp; As our workforce matures, we may not be able to&nbsp;sustain the impact of the resulting higher wage rates if competition or other&nbsp;economic conditions do not permit us to achieve&nbsp;necessary revenues.</p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <i><u>We may not be able to successfully negotiate new collective bargaining agreements on satisfactory terms.</u></i></font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></b> Approximately 73% of our employees are covered by collective bargaining agreements.&nbsp; We are currently in negotiations with our dispatchers and
mechanics whose contracts became amendable in 2009.&nbsp; We will begin negotiations with our flight attendants and pilots as their contracts become amendable in 2010.&nbsp; Deterioration in our labor relationships could significantly impact our operations and
financial results.&nbsp; Our contract with our production workers does not have a term but salaries are typically renegotiated each year.&nbsp; We may not be able to successfully negotiate new collective bargaining agreements on satisfactory terms.</p>

<p><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></i> <b><i><u><font size="2">Amendments to the terms of the convertible notes increased our obligations and put our assets at risk.</font></u></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In August 2008, we commenced a repurchase offer for the 4.25% convertible notes due 2023 (the &ldquo;Original 4.25% Convertible Notes due 2023&rdquo;) and provide
written notice to the trustee of our intention to pay the repurchase price wholly in shares of our common stock (the &ldquo;Notes Exchange Offer&rdquo;).&nbsp; As a result and pursuant to the terms of the exchange offer, the Company issued 16,382,498 shares (reverse
split adjusted) of common stock in payment of the repurchase price for the $59.7 million principal amount of the Original 4.25% Convertible Notes due 2023 validly tendered and to settle accrued and unpaid interest due August 1, 2008.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Following the completion of the Notes Exchange Offer, $68.5 million aggregate principal of the Original 4.25% Convertible Notes due 2023 remained outstanding.&nbsp; As
previously disclosed, we have unilaterally amended the indenture governing the Original 4.25% Convertible Notes due 2023 in order to provide improved terms and additional flexibility for the note holders remaining after the exchange offer, including:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<div align="center">

<td height="17" valign="top">

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Noteholders of record on August 2, 2008, automatically began to receive the benefits of the supplemental indenture that become effective the same day.&nbsp; From August
2, 2008 forward, the notes are referred to as the &ldquo;11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023&rdquo;.&nbsp; The terms of the 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 could adversely affect our financial condition and make it more difficult to satisfy our
obligations under the notes and our other contractual and commercial commitments.&nbsp; The amendments also increased the cash required to service the interest on the notes.&nbsp; If our business does not generate sufficient cash flow from operations in the future,
we may be required to take actions such as curtailing our business activities, reducing capital expenditures, selling assets, incurring additional debt or seeking bankruptcy protection.&nbsp; We may not be able to accomplish any of these actions on terms acceptable
to us, or at all.&nbsp; In addition, if we are unable to repay our obligations under the notes, the trustee could seek to foreclose on the assets securing the notes.&nbsp; As of December 31, 2009, $52.1 million of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 remain
outstanding.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><i><u>Conversion of our convertible notes could dilute the ownership interest of existing stockholders.</u></i></b></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> <font size="2">On August 1, 2011, holders of our outstanding 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 may require us to repurchase their notes.&nbsp; We may pay
the repurchase price in cash or in stock.&nbsp; The conversion of some or all of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 would dilute the ownership interests of existing stockholders.&nbsp; Any sales in the public market of the common stock issuable upon
conversion of the notes could adversely affect prevailing market prices of our common stock.&nbsp; In addition, the existence of the notes may encourage short selling by market participants because the conversion of the notes could further depress the price of our
common stock.&nbsp; Finally, i</font><font size="2">f we do not continue to meet the listing standards with the NYSE, we could be subject to delisting, which would constitute a default under our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 and could result in the
obligation to repay the notes in cash at par.&nbsp; There is currently $52.1 million aggregate principal amount outstanding of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We operate a single fleet type produced by a single manufacturer; consequently, our operations could be materially adversely affected by:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></i></b> Conversely, if we choose to operate another aircraft type in the future, for a time we will not have the maintenance expertise we have acquired with
our current fleet, training costs would increase, and parts and inventory costs would rise.</p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Maintenance costs will likely increase as the average age of our fleet increases.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; As the average age of our fleet increases, our aircraft maintenance costs will likely increase.&nbsp; We perform routine inspection and maintenance of our aircraft
engines and airframes at intervals required by the FAA.&nbsp;</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Additionally, under the Rolls Agreement, we are charged a fixed rate based on flight hours incurred during a month.&nbsp; The rates are subject to annual revisions based
on specified labor and material indices.&nbsp; We also have power-by-the-hour agreements with other vendors to cover various components and systems on our aircraft.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our average maintenance costs under these agreements could increase and adversely impact our results of operations. We may also incur increased maintenance costs if we
have to address any new FAA or Embraer maintenance directives.&nbsp;</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; For the majority of our aircraft not covered in the Amended Continental CPA, we expect to incur unreimbursable costs related to the replacement of certain life-limited
parts, primarily engine parts, in the near future as these parts approach their cycle limits.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Reductions in insurance coverage or increases in rates could adversely impact our operations and financial results.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The terrorist attacks of 2001 led to a significant increase in insurance premiums, as well as a decrease in the coverage available to commercial air carriers. We carry
insurance for public liability, passenger liability, property damage and damage to our aircraft.&nbsp; The Homeland Security Act of 2002 currently requires the federal government to provide third party, passenger, and hull war-risk insurance coverage to commercial
air carriers through August 31, 2010.&nbsp; If any of our insurance programs terminated, the Company would likely face a material increase in the cost of war-risk insurance.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Consolidations in our industry can adversely impact our current business strategy.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><i><u><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></u></i></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; There have been numerous mergers and acquisitions within the U.S airline industry since its deregulation in 1978, and there may be additional mergers and
acquisitions in the future.&nbsp; Any airline industry consolidation could substantially alter the competitive landscape and may result in changes in our business strategy.&nbsp; Consolidation involving legacy carriers in our industry could, in the long run, result
in the reduction of capacity for network-feed services to be provided by the regional carriers, which could have a material adverse effect on us.</font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Our cost structure may not be competitive with some of our competitors.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our costs are mainly driven by the flight schedule determined by Continental, Continental&rsquo;s own cost structure or factors that are outside our control, or in some
instances even Continental&rsquo;s control (such as aircraft rent, fuel, insurance and property taxes).&nbsp; As a significant portion of our costs are wages that are contractually agreed with our labor work groups, we may not be able to restructure our costs
effectively to compete with other carriers.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Our business is subject to extensive government regulation and we may incur additional costs to comply with such regulations.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our business is subject to extensive government regulation.&nbsp; As evidenced by the enactment of the ATSA, airlines are subject to extensive regulatory and legal
compliance requirements that can or may result in significant costs.&nbsp; The FAA and other governmental agencies such as the EPA from time to time issue directives and other regulations relating to the maintenance and operation of aircraft that require significant
expenditures.&nbsp; Some requirements cover, among other things, excessive tarmac delays, security measures, collision avoidance systems, potable water standards, noise abatement and other environmental matters, commuter aircraft safety and increased inspections and
maintenance procedures conducted on older aircraft.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We expect to continue incurring expenses to comply with these regulations.&nbsp; In addition, if any of these regulations, including the new rule adopted by the DOT
limiting airline tarmac delays, caused us to cancel flights, it would result in a reduction in our revenue.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Other regulatory actions that may be taken in the future by the U.S. government to address climate change or limit the emission of greenhouse gases by the
aviation sector are unknown at this time.&nbsp;</font> <font color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;</font> <font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">Concerns about climate change and greenhouse gas emissions, in particular, may result in the imposition of additional
legislation or regulation.&nbsp;&nbsp; Such legislative or regulatory action by the U.S., state or foreign governments currently or in the future may adversely affect our business and financial results.&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Additional laws, regulations, taxes and airport rates and charges are proposed from time to time that could significantly increase the cost of airline operations or
reduce revenue.&nbsp; Such laws, taxes and regulations have affected all facets of our operations from security at airports, restrictions on landing, take-off, routes, restrictions on international routes (which can change suddenly depending on the current
arrangements between the United States and the foreign governments), and increases in landing fees and other airport facility charges.&nbsp; We cannot be certain that current laws or regulations, or laws or regulations enacted in the future, will not adversely affect
us.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><i><u>We may be adversely affected by factors beyond our control, including weather conditions and the availability and cost of fuel</u></i></b>.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; As climate changes cause more severe weather occurrences, including periods of fog, icy conditions, storms, hurricanes or other adverse weather conditions, our
operations could be materially impacted if flights were significantly reduced.&nbsp; Under the Amended Continental CPA and the United Express Agreement, we are not fully protected against cancellations due to weather or air traffic control restrictions, which could
adversely affect our operating results and our financial condition.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Additionally, in operating our aircraft for other airlines or under charter contracts we may be exposed to the volatility of fuel prices.&nbsp; Both the cost and
availability of fuel are subject to various economic and political factors and events occurring throughout the world.&nbsp; Significant changes or extended periods of high fuel cost or fuel supply disruptions could materially affect our operating results.&nbsp; Our
ability to pass on increased fuel costs through contract pricing is limited by several factors, including economic and competitive conditions.&nbsp; Additionally, under the Amended Continental CPA and the United Express Agreement, if the unavailability of fuel caused
us to cancel flights, our incentive revenue would be reduced.&nbsp; The cost and availability of adequate supplies of fuel could have a material adverse effect on our operating results and our financial condition in the future.</font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Our reliance on technology and the technology of our operating partners could be harmful in the event of system failure.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><u><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></u></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We rely heavily on automated systems and technology to operate our business, including flight operations and telecommunications.&nbsp; Any disruptions in
these systems or the systems of our operating partners due to internal failures of technology or external interruptions, such as power outages, could result in the loss of critical data and/or cancellation of flights and have an adverse effect on our results of
operations.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <u>Our operations and financial condition could be adversely affected as a result of an aviation accident.</u></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; An accident or incident involving one of our aircraft could involve repair or replacement of a damaged aircraft and its consequential temporary or permanent loss from
service, as well as significant potential claims of injured passengers and others.&nbsp; In the event of an accident, our liability insurance may not be adequate and we may be forced to bear substantial losses from the accident.&nbsp; Substantial claims resulting
from an accident in excess of our related insurance coverage would harm operational and financial results.&nbsp; Moreover, any aircraft accident or incident could create a public perception that we are less safe or reliable than other airlines.</font></p>

<p><a name="facilities"></a><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Facilities</font></u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><u>Airports</u></b></font></p>

<p><font size="3" face="Times New Roman"></font></p>

<p><font size="3" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> <font size="2" face="Arial">We lease all of our airport passenger facilities either directly with the airport authorities or in some cases, through
arrangements with Continental, on a net-rental basis.&nbsp; Our largest operational centers are at Houston&rsquo;s George Bush Intercontinental Airport, which is approximately 155,000 square feet, with 33 passenger loading bridges and 15 hardstand positions in
Terminal B and 4 passenger loading bridges and 7 hardstand positions in Terminal D; Cleveland&rsquo;s Hopkins International Airport, of which we have approximately 106,000 square feet and 12 passenger loading bridges and 6 hardstand positions in Terminal D; and
Newark Liberty International Airport, where we operate out of Continental&rsquo;s Terminal A with up to 14 passenger loading bridges and 2 hardstand positions.&nbsp; In addition, at each of Continental's three domestic hubs and many other locations, our passenger and
baggage handling space is provided by Continental on varying terms dependent on the prevailing practice at each airport.&nbsp; If the Amended Continental CPA were terminated, we might be required to vacate the terminal facilities (or all facilities if the termination
resulted from our material breach of the agreement) that are subleased to us by Continental, and to use commercially reasonable efforts to transfer to Continental or its designee any lease in our name.&nbsp; For further discussion of our airport facilities, slots and
route authorities, refer to Item 1, <i>Business.</i>&nbsp; For a period of five years following the termination of the Amended Continental CPA, if we wanted to transfer our interests in any of our facilities used to fulfill our obligations under the agreement,
Continental would need to consent to the transfer (where Continental is the sublessor) and has a right of first refusal to acquire our interests in those facilities that we lease from parties other than Continental.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; As of December 31, 2009, we continue to lease approximately 5,000 square feet of terminal space including one gate at the Will Rodgers World Airport in Oklahoma City,
Oklahoma; 2,000 square feet of terminal space at the Louisville International Airport in Louisville, Kentucky and 1,668 square feet of&nbsp;terminal space and one gate at the Boise Air Terminal in Boise, Idaho previously associated with our Branded
Flying<b>.&nbsp;</b> Our facilities team has been very aggressive in working to sublease or terminate the leases associated with the remaining Branded Flying lease obligations which expire between June 2010 and December 2010.&nbsp; All expenses associated with the
leases were recorded in our Consolidated Statement of Operations for the year ended December 31, 2008 after Branded Flying operations were suspended.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></i> <u>Corporate Offices and Other</u></b></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our Houston headquarters building is comprised of executive, administrative and operations control departments, occupying approximately 42,000 square feet of leased
space.&nbsp; We also lease a second building that consists of 18,000 square feet for executive and administrative staff and 50,000 square feet of production and warehouse space utilized by InTech.&nbsp; To reduce overhead expenses, we moved executive and
administrative staff from our second building utilized by InTech to our headquarters building and are working to sublease the space.&nbsp; Additionally, we lease a 57,000 square foot training center containing numerous simulators, training devices and corresponding
training and administrative staff.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></i> <u>Maintenance Facilities</u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In addition to our airport passenger facilities, we currently operate six major maintenance facilities (hangars/shops) in Houston, Cleveland, Newark, Knoxville,
Shreveport and Richmond, as well as four satellite line maintenance facilities in other cities.&nbsp; Additionally, XJT Mexico, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Holdings, owns three buildings consisting of approximately 96,000 square feet of hangar space and 3,000
square feet of administrative space in Saltillo, Mexico that is leased to Saltillo for use in its aircraft painting business.&nbsp; We are responsible for maintenance, taxes, insurance and other facility-related expenses and services at these facilities.</font></p>

<div align="center"><font size="2" face="Arial"></font>

<p><a name="item3"></a><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Item 3.&nbsp; Legal Proceedings</font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In July 2009, we entered into a settlement agreement related to our auction rate securities (&ldquo;ARS&rdquo;) litigation against RBC Capital Markets
Corporation et al. (collectively &ldquo;RBC&rdquo;) with respect to certain ARS purchased from RBC. Among other terms, the settlement agreement provided for RBC to immediately repurchase ARS&nbsp;with an aggregate par value of $18,000,000 it sold to ExpressJet for
87.5% of par value.&nbsp; Additionally, if within twelve months of the date of the execution of the settlement agreement, any of the ARS is redeemed or refinanced by its issuer and RBC is paid a sum representing greater than 87.5% of the par value of that ARS, we are
to&nbsp;be paid&nbsp;a sum representing the difference between (1)&nbsp;87.5% of the par value of that ARS and (2) the sum actually received by RBC.&nbsp; As part of the settlement agreement, we dismissed our lawsuit against RBC and released claims related to
RBC&rsquo;s sale of the ARS to us.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In September 2009, we initiated litigation against Bank of America Corporation et al. (&ldquo;BOA&rdquo;) related to ARS that BOA sold to ExpressJet in January
2008.&nbsp; During the fourth quarter of 2009, we consummated four separate transactions pursuant to which we sold $5.0 million of ARS purchased from BOA for 90.5% of the face value of the securities, $10.0 million of ARS purchased from BOA for 90.0% of the face
value of the securities and $4.95 million of ARS purchased from BOA for 93.0% of the face value of the securities.&nbsp; As of December 31, 2009, the aggregate par value of our remaining ARS holdings purchased from BOA was $1.1 million.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In October 2009, we finalized an agreement with Flight Services and Systems, Inc. (&ldquo;FSS&rdquo;) pursuant to which, among other things, FSS repurchased our 44%
interest and each party granted the other a mutual release of all present and future claims against the other.&nbsp; The purchase price received from FSS consisted of $1.0 million and a promissory note in the amount of $600,000, which note is payable in sixty (60)
equal monthly installments of principal plus interest.&nbsp; The first payment was received in December 2009.&nbsp; Our investment in FSS totaled $1.2 million immediately prior to this agreement.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We are a defendant in various lawsuits arising in the ordinary course of our business.&nbsp; While the outcome of these lawsuits and proceedings cannot be predicted with
certainty and could have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations or cash flows, we believe that the ultimate disposition of these suits will not have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations or cash
flows.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><a name="environm"></a><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Environmental Proceedings</font></u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We are and may from time to time become involved in environmental matters, including the investigation and/or remediation of environmental conditions at properties we
use or were previously used by us.&nbsp; We are not, however, currently subject to any environmental cleanup orders imposed by regulatory authorities, nor do we have any active investigations or remediation at this time.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <a name="OLE_LINK11"></a><a name="OLE_LINK12">In July 2005, our Board of Directors authorized the expenditure of up to $30 million to repurchase shares of our common
stock.&nbsp; In February 2006, the Board authorized the inclusion of our Original 4.25% Convertible Notes due 2023 (now our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023), within the previously announced program.&nbsp; Our Board authorized an additional $15 million in
2008 and $10 million in 2009 to be utilized for purchases within this program.&nbsp; Repurchases have been made from time to time in the open market and in privately negotiated transactions; the timing of any repurchases under the program depends on a variety of
factors, including market conditions, and may be suspended or discontinued at any time.</a></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In 2009, we repurchased 3.0 million shares of our common stock and $8.7 million par value of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023.&nbsp; As of December 31,
2009, a balance of $9.7 million remained in the program for additional repurchases.</font></p>

<p><a name="Item6"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Item 6.&nbsp; Selected Financial Data</font></b></a></p>



<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; This selected financial data should be read together with the <i>Consolidated Financial Statements, Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements and Management&rsquo;s
Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations</i> included in this report.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In 2009, ExpressJet continued to transition its business by focusing on contractual flying arrangements.&nbsp; <font color="black">In addition, we placed emphasis on
improving our balance sheet in light of the pressures of industry-wide capacity reductions and continued difficulties in the global economy.&nbsp; These</font> efforts included the repurchase of $8.7 million of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 in the
open market, which reduced the outstanding principal balance of our convertible notes from $60.8 million as of December 31, 2008 to $52.1 million as of December 31, 2009.&nbsp; We also repurchased 3.0 million shares of our common stock in 2009.&nbsp; In late 2009, we
began to reallocate aircraft within our fleet to immediately support existing capacity needs of United under the United Express Agreement.&nbsp; Additionally, revenues increased over 40% in 2009 within our Corporate Aviation (charter) division.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The following selected financial data, excluding operating statistics, have been derived from our audited financial statements.&nbsp; The financial information included
in this report is not necessarily indicative of our future results of operations, financial position and cash flows.&nbsp; For a discussion of some of the key factors that could have an adverse effect on our results of operations, financial position and cash flows,
refer to Item 1A, <i>Risk Factors</i>.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; As discussed in</font> <font size="2" face="Arial">Note 1, &ldquo;Adjustments and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies,&rdquo; in <i>Notes to Consolidated
Financial Statements</i>, our Consolidated Financial Statements for each period presented have been adjusted for the retrospective application of the Cash Conversion Subsections of the Financial Accounting Standards Board&rsquo;s (&ldquo;FASB&rdquo;) Accounting
Standards Codification (&ldquo;ASC&rdquo;) Subtopic 470-20, &ldquo;Debt with Conversion and Other Options &ndash; Cash Conversion&rdquo; (&ldquo;Debt with Conversion Options Subtopic&rdquo;).</font></p>

</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Revenue passenger miles are the number of scheduled miles flown by revenue passengers.</font></p>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(2)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Available seat miles are the number of passenger seats available multiplied by the number of scheduled miles those seats are flown.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(3)&nbsp;</font></p>

</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(4)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Operating cost per available seat mile is operating costs divided by available seat miles.&nbsp; The reimbursable expenses are different under the terms of the Amended Continental CPA versus the Original Continental CPA, and therefore
costs are inconsistent with prior periods, beginning July 2008.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(5)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Block hours are the hours from gate departure to gate arrival.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(6)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Operating cost per block hour is operating costs divided by block hours.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(7)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Beginning in 2007, our fuel activity includes purchases to support our various business platforms outside of the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; These purchases were executed through agreements with independent third parties.&nbsp; Under
the Amended Continental CPA, Continental is directly responsible for the cost of providing fuel for all flights operating as Continental Express; therefore, the related fuel expense is no longer included in our Consolidated Statements of Operations for periods
subsequent to July 1, 2008.&nbsp; Prior to July 1, 2008 under our fuel purchase agreement with Continental, fuel and fuel tax expense were reconciled to the lower of the actual costs or the agreed-upon caps.&nbsp; From 2003 through July 1, 2008, our caps on fuel and
fuel taxes, for aircraft operating under the Original Continental CPA, were 66.0 cents and 5.2 cents per gallon, respectively.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(8)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Average daily utilization of each aircraft is the average number of block hours per day that an aircraft in revenue service is operated.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Item 7.&nbsp; <a name="item7"></a>Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations</font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The information contained in this section has been derived from, is provided as a supplement to, and should be read in conjunction with our Consolidated Financial
Statements and the accompanying notes thereto contained in &ldquo;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&rdquo; of this report.&nbsp; This section contains forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties.&nbsp; Our actual results may differ
materially from those expressed or implied in these forward-looking statements as a result of various factors, including those described in &ldquo;Forward-Looking Statements&rdquo; and in Item 1A, <i>Risk Factors</i>.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><a name="overview"></a><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Overview</font></u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The following Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations ("MD&amp;A") is intended to help the reader understand our operations
and our current business environment.&nbsp; MD&amp;A is provided as a supplement to &mdash; and should be read in conjunction with &mdash; our Consolidated Financial Statements and the accompanying notes thereto contained in &ldquo;Financial Statements and
Supplementary Data" of this report. This overview summarizes MD&amp;A, which includes the following sections:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<div align="center">
<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="672">
<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Our Business &mdash;</font></i> a general description of our business, including our business segments; our objective; focus areas; and challenges and risks of our business.</p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates &mdash;</font></i> a discussion of accounting policies that require critical judgments and estimates.</p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>

<p><u><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></u></p>

<p><a name="ourbusiness"></a><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Our Business</font></u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></i></b> <font size="2" face="Arial">We are one of the largest regional airlines in the world.&nbsp; We currently operate 244 Embraer regional jets and have
over 5,600 employees.&nbsp; We have three primary categories of operations:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<div align="center">
<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="672">
<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Scheduled regional airline service for mainline partners;</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Dedicated charter operations; and</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Third-party aviation services provider of airport ground handling, aircraft maintenance, aircraft refurbishment (interiors and paint) work and aircraft cleaning.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our main business focuses on providing regional airline service that feeds passengers to our partner&rsquo;s hub airports.&nbsp; Due to the fact that our service is
provided under our partner&rsquo;s brand name, the ExpressJet brand is relatively unknown to the public.&nbsp; During 2009, our primary partner was Continental, a member of the Star Alliance.&nbsp; We are an integral part of Continental&rsquo;s network, bringing
customers to and from its hubs in Houston, Newark and Cleveland who connect to or from their flights.&nbsp; As a result of the low cost per trip for 50-seat regional jets when compared to alternative aircraft, ExpressJet is able to bring jet service to many areas
that would not otherwise have air service.&nbsp; These smaller communities gain non-stop air service to partner hubs along with connections to worldwide destinations from the hubs that ExpressJet feeds.&nbsp; During 2009, we completed 349,733 departures as
Continental Express under the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; In November 2009, we added a second long-term partner when United, another member of the Star Alliance, announced a multi-year arrangement with us for 22 aircraft flying as United Express pursuant to the
United Express Agreement.&nbsp; The agreement will have an initial term of three years for 11 aircraft and two years for the remaining 11 aircraft, and will have a renewal option, at United&rsquo;s election, for additional periods up to a total term of five
years.&nbsp; From an industry perspective during 2009, we were the third largest regional airline based on passengers enplaned behind only American Eagle and SkyWest.</font></p>

<div align="center"><font size="2" face="Arial"></font>
<hr size="2" width="100%" noshade color="black" align="center" />

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We operated a total of six aircraft under the United Express Agreement as of December&nbsp;31, 2009 and a total of 16 aircraft under the United Express Agreement as of
February 17, 2010.&nbsp; The remaining six long-term aircraft will begin operating under the United Express Agreement on March 1, 2010.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; From May 2010 through December 2010, we will fly up to ten additional aircraft on a short-term basis for United Express in the current ExpressJet livery.&nbsp; United
will have the option to renew the operation of these aircraft for up to four additional periods of not less than thirty days per renewal period.&nbsp; United must notify us of its intention to renew for the initial renewal period no later than June 15, 2010 for the
first six supplemental aircraft and August 15, 2010 for the remaining four additional aircraft.&nbsp; We have also agreed to a framework that would allow United to extend the renewal notice deadline for each aircraft upon certain terms and
conditions.&nbsp;</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In 2010, our continued exceptional performance will be a key to our success.&nbsp; Historically, we perform at or near the top of the rankings for fewest carrier caused
delays or cancellations as measured by the DOT.&nbsp; An industry-leading performance for this metric is key for two reasons:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<div align="center">
<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="672">

</td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Our mainline partners, Continental and United, depend on us to provide exceptionally reliable operations to complement their brand by providing seamless customer service, evidenced by few customer complaints and passenger survey scores;
and</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&bull;&nbsp;</font></b></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">We are paid on a per block hour basis by our mainline partners.&nbsp; If the flight does not operate, we do not earn revenue.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We have been a leader in reliability within the airline industry regarding carrier-caused delays since we became a DOT reporting carrier in 2002.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In addition to providing regional airline service for legacy carriers, we operate one of the world&rsquo;s largest dedicated charter passenger fleets through our
Corporate Aviation (charter) division.&nbsp; A core advantage of this fleet of aircraft is the highly competitive lease rates as provided to us under the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; In 2009, we operated a dedicated charter fleet of 30 aircraft in our Corporate
Aviation (charter) division.&nbsp; In 2010, the number of aircraft in this division will fluctuate between six aircraft and 16 aircraft, depending on the number of aircraft needed to support flying for United under the United Express Agreement.&nbsp; With a
near-perfect operational record, we spent 2009 focusing on improving the margins associated with these operations.&nbsp; We expect these efforts, coupled with a smaller number of aircraft dedicated to our Corporate Aviation (charter) division in 2010, should improve
our returns in this line of business.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our fleet of 244 aircraft is planned to be allocated as follows during 2010:</font></p>

facility in Mexico and an aircraft interiors shop in Houston.&nbsp; We operate each of these businesses under ExpressJet Services.&nbsp; In addition to offering these services to our partners and other industry participants, we also use these services as a vehicle to
diversify our revenue streams and control costs associated with our flying operations.&nbsp; For example, each of the aircraft utilized under the United Express Agreement will be painted at our aircraft paint facility.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><u>Our Business Segments</u></b></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; For the year ended December 31, 2009, <font color="black">ExpressJet had two reportable segments which are the basis of our internal financial reporting:&nbsp; Contract
Flying and Aviation Services.</font></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Contract Flying includes flying conducted in our Corporate Aviation (charter) division, under the Amended Continental CPA and under the United Express
Agreement.&nbsp; Under Contract Flying, revenues are contractually determined, eliminating our exposure to fluctuations in fuel prices, fare competition and passenger volumes.&nbsp; Under these arrangements, our partners bear the revenue risk and cost of marketing
and distribution on our aircraft while we are responsible for the operation and maintenance of the aircraft.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Aviation Services includes our ground-handling services pursuant to contracts with Continental and other airlines at airport locations across the United
States, as well as those performed by ExpressJet Services.&nbsp;</font> Under ExpressJet Services&rsquo; brand, we paint aircraft and repair composite structures, aircraft interiors (including refurbishment of seats, galleys, lavatories and panels) and thrust
reversers throughout our four facilities in the United States and Mexico.</p>

<p><i><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"></font></i></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our goal is to return to profitability by efficiently utilizing our assets and through a strong commitment by our management and employees.&nbsp; Our plans for returning
to profitability include:</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><i>Contract Flying &ndash; Amended Continental CPA</i></b></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A significant portion of our revenue and cash flows is attributable to the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; Under the Amended Continental CPA, Airlines operates flights on
behalf of Continental as Continental Express.&nbsp; For a detailed discussion of the Amended Continental CPA, refer to Note 2, &ldquo;Contract Flying,&rdquo; in <i>Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements.</i></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Contract Flying &ndash; United Express Agreement</font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></b> <font size="2" face="Arial">In February 2010, we entered into the United Express Agreement with United to<b></b></font><font size="2" face="Arial">fly 22
ERJ-145 aircraft as United Express beginning December 1, 2009.&nbsp; The United Express Agreement has an initial term expiring on April 30, 2012 for 11 aircraft and on April 30, 2013 for the remaining 11 aircraft, and contains a renewal option, at United&rsquo;s
election, for additional periods up to a total term of five years.&nbsp; Under this arrangement, United must notify ExpressJet of its intention to renew each group of aircraft not less than six month&rsquo;s prior to the end of the term for such aircraft.&nbsp;
Additionally in February 2010, we entered into the First Amendment to the United Express Agreement with United, pursuant to which we will fly up to ten additional aircraft for United in the current ExpressJet livery from May 2010 through December 2010.</font><font
size="2">&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> <font size="2" face="Arial">United will have the option to renew these supplemental aircraft for up to four additional periods of not less than thirty days per renewal period.&nbsp; Under this arrangement, United must notify ExpressJet of
its intention to renew for the initial renewal period no later than June 15, 2010 for the first six supplemental aircraft and August 15, 2010 for the remaining four additional aircraft.&nbsp; In an effort to provide United with increased flexibility, the amendment
allows United to extend the renewal deadline for each aircraft upon certain terms and conditions.&nbsp; If United elects not to extend the term of the supplemental aircraft, the ten aircraft will be removed from service, and placed into the Corporate Aviation
(charter) operation.&nbsp; For a detailed discussion of the United Express Agreement, refer to Item 1, <i>Business.</i></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"><br clear="all" />

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> <b><i>Contract Flying &ndash; Corporate Aviation</i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" color="black" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font> Towards the end of 2008, we expanded our Corporate Aviation (charter) division to 30 aircraft.&nbsp; In 2009, these aircraft were subject to
long-term agreements and other ad-hoc charter service arrangements.&nbsp; Our Corporate Aviation (charter) division continues to focus on corporate shuttles, entertainment / sports, and government businesses.&nbsp; Certain Corporate Aviation (charter) customers
typically provide deposits for flights based on a percentage of estimated charges to be incurred.&nbsp; These prepayments are held in escrow and recorded as restricted cash and deferred revenue until the flights are completed.&nbsp; At that time we recognize the
associated revenue and release the funds from escrow into our cash account.</p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The aircraft in the Corporate Aviation (charter) division are flown under Airlines&rsquo; operating certificate issued by the FAA.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; All of our seats for these aircraft are leather, memory foam cushioned seats and include XM Satellite Radio with over 100 channels of audio entertainment.&nbsp; In
addition to our basic amenities (such as providing blankets to each passenger and standard catering) customized flight service options give customers an opportunity to create a unique flight experience.</font></p>

<p><i><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></i></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Aviation Services</font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Aviation Services includes our ground-handling services pursuant to our contracts with Continental and other airlines at airport locations across the United States, as
well as ExpressJet Services.&nbsp; We will continue to leverage our operational expertise developed from this business segment to cost-effectively serve our current customers and attract new customers.&nbsp; Need to add in aircraft cleaning contract.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><u>Our 2010 Outlook</u></b></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The International Air Transport Association (&ldquo;IATA&rdquo;) reported December and full-year 2009 demand statistics for international scheduled air traffic that
showed the industry ending 2009 with the largest ever post-war decline. Passenger demand for the full year was down 3.5% with an average load factor of 75.6%.&nbsp; IATA predicted that the airline industry permanently lost 2.5 years of growth in passenger markets and
that revenue improvements will be at a much slower pace than the demand growth.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Seasonally adjusted demand figures for December compared to November 2009 indicate a 1.6% rise in passenger traffic.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; December 2009 passenger demand recorded a 4.5% improvement compared to December 2008, with a load factor of 77.6%.&nbsp; While this is an 8.4% demand improvement from
the February 2009 low point, it is still 3.4 points below the early 2008 peak.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The economic recovery and continued improvement in passenger demand, as described above by IATA, will be a key to our success during 2010.&nbsp; United currently is
projecting a more aggressive use of regional jets, so adding this flying during 2010 should help increase the productivity and utilization of our aircraft to pre-recessionary levels.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Continental and United each provide investor updates regularly and discuss their capacity guidance and are the best resource for capacity expectations.&nbsp; On January
21, 2010, Continental published an investor update and indicated regional capacity expectations to decline 0.2% for 2010.&nbsp; Despite lower capacity guidance, we believe that we should be more productive on a per aircraft basis as we will operate eight fewer planes
(206 versus 214) under this agreement in 2010.&nbsp; On January 27, 2010, United published their investor update and indicated 6.3% - 7.3% regional affiliate capacity growth.&nbsp; Both of these estimates are based on available seat miles.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; We believe that additional opportunities may present themselves during the year as Continental continues to develop its network within the Star Alliance, of which United
is a long-standing member.</font></p>

<p><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates</font></u></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Our Consolidated Financial Statements have been prepared in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles <font color=
"black">(&ldquo;GAAP&rdquo;)</font>.&nbsp; The preparation of these financial statements requires us to make estimates and judgments that affect reported amounts and related disclosures.&nbsp; We have identified the accounting policies and estimates below as critical
to our business operations and understanding of our results of operations.&nbsp; The SEC has defined critical accounting policies and estimates as the ones that are most important to the presentation of a Company&rsquo;s financial condition and results and require
the Company to make its most difficult and subjective judgments, often as a result of the need to make estimates of matters that are inherently uncertain.&nbsp; For all of these estimates, we caution that future events rarely develop exactly as forecasted, and the
best estimates routinely require judgment.&nbsp; The discussion below is not intended to be a comprehensive list of our accounting estimates and policies.&nbsp; For a detailed discussion on the application of our accounting policies, refer to Note 1,
&ldquo;Adjustments and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies,&rdquo; in <i>Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements.</i></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Effective July 1, 2009, the <font color="black">FASB ASC became the exclusive authoritative reference for non-governmental GAAP in the United States.&nbsp; The ASC
became the only level of authoritative GAAP and eliminated the previous four-level hierarchy.&nbsp; Our accounting policies were not affected by the conversion to ASC.&nbsp; However, references to specific accounting standards in the footnotes to our Consolidated
Financial Statements have been changed to refer to the appropriate section of ASC.</font></font></p>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Revenue Recognition<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Contract Revenues.&nbsp;</font></i></b> We recognize our operating revenue under contractual arrangements, such as the Amended Continental CPA and certain long-term Corporate Aviation agreements, pursuant to the terms of the
contracts.&nbsp; Operating revenues from these contracts have been classified as passenger revenue.&nbsp; Under the Amended Continental CPA, we derive our revenue based on fixed block hour rates multiplied by the block hours flown for the period thereby reducing or
eliminating the risk of misinterpretation of the agreement.</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Revenue Recognition</font></b><br />
<br />
 <b><i>Contract Revenues.</i></b>&nbsp; We recognize as revenue compensation received from Continental for reimbursement of certain trued-up costs, when agreed to by the parties, as such amounts may be subject to contract interpretation.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Revenue Recognition</font></b><br />
<br />
 <b><i>Contract Revenues.</i></b>&nbsp; After a mutually agreed upon application has been reached, our methodology used to record revenue as related to true-up costs, substantially reduces the need for estimates and assumptions.&nbsp; We applied this methodology
consistently throughout 2009 and we do not expect any material changes to that methodology going forward.</p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Spare Parts and Supplies<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Inventories, expendable parts and supplies relating to flight equipment are carried at average acquisition cost and are expensed when used.&nbsp; Inventories are carried at the lower of amortized cost or net realizable value.&nbsp; The
adequacy of our allowance for obsolescence requires a high degree of judgment.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Spare Parts and Supplies</font></b><br />
<br />
 Our allowance for obsolescence related to inventory is provided over the remaining useful life of the related aircraft, plus allowance for spare parts currently identified as excess.&nbsp; Part of the calculation for this reserve is based on historical
experience.&nbsp; In addition, we may reserve for additional obsolescence when current available market data indicate a decline in the fair value of parts or if we deem parts as excess inventory.</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Spare Parts and Supplies</font></b><br />
<br />
 As of December 31, 2009, our allowance for obsolescence related to our spare parts and supplies was approximately $14.4 million.</p>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Fair Value Measurements<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Cash and Short-term Investments.&nbsp;</font></i></b> <i>ASC Topic 820, &ldquo;Fair Value Measurement and Disclosures<b>&rdquo;</b> (&ldquo;ASC Topic 820&rdquo;)</i>provides a consistent definition of fair value which focuses on
exit price and prioritizes, within a measurement of fair value, the use of market based inputs over entity-specific inputs.&nbsp; ASC Topic 820 also establishes a three-level hierarchy for fair value measurements based on the transparency of inputs to the valuation
of an asset or liability as of the measurement date.&nbsp; As of December 31, 2009 we held cash equivalents and short-term investments in ARS that were required to be measured at fair value.&nbsp; We determine the fair value of our cash equivalents and ARS using
inputs which are unobservable and significant to the fair value measurement such as the timing of expected future cash flows, underlying collateralization, creditworthiness of the counterparties, and a discount rate that accounts for relevant market conditions.&nbsp;
In addition, in April 2009 the FASB issued new guidance which modified the requirements for recognizing other-than-temporary-impaired debt securities.&nbsp; As such, any declines in fair value are evaluated against this new standard to determine if the declines are
other-than-temporary.</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Fair Value Measurements</font></b><font size="1"><br />
<br />
</font> <b><i>Cash and Short-term Investments.&nbsp;</i></b> We determine the fair value of our ARS using a discounted cash flow model and significant unobservable inputs.&nbsp; Our model contains uncertainties because it requires management to make assumptions and
to apply judgment to estimate discount rates, anticipated maturity, industry and economic factors and other key metrics.</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Fair Value Measurements</font></b><font size="1"><br />
<br />
</font> <b><i>Cash and Short-term Investments</i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">We consistently applied the fair value approach to our ARS throughout 2009 and recorded other-than-temporary losses of $0.1 million as &ldquo;Impairment charges on investments&rdquo; in our Consolidated Statement of Operations.&nbsp;
Recoveries in fair value of $0.7 million were credited to other comprehensive income on our Consolidated Balance Sheets in 2009.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Convertible Secured Notes<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">As referred to in Note 1, &ldquo;Adjustments and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies,&rdquo; in <i>Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements</i>, our convertible notes have been accounted for pursuant to the Debt with Conversion
Options Subtopic in which the liability and equity components are separately accounted for to reflect an estimated effective interest rate as if the debt instrument had been issued on a standalone basis. &nbsp; This resulting discount is amortized over the expected
term of our Convertible Secured Notes or through 2011. &nbsp;Any gains or losses upon extinguishment or derecognition are recorded in the period they occur.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Convertible Secured Notes</font></b><font size="1"><br />
<br />
</font> We determine the estimated value of the liability component based on market information for standalone debt instruments which is subject to significant judgment due to the current credit crisis.</p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Convertible Secured Notes</font></b><font size="1"><br />
<br />
</font> In 2009, we repurchased $8.7 million par value of our 11.25% Convertible Secured Notes due 2023 which resulted in gains on extinguishment of debt of $1.0 million within the scope of the Debt with Conversion Options Subtopic.&nbsp; Such gains were calculated
as the difference between the fair value of the liability component immediately prior to extinguishment and its book value.</p>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Long-Lived Assets<br />
 </font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Long-lived assets, primarily consisting of investments in other entities and flight and ground equipment assets are evaluated for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying value may not be
recoverable.&nbsp; When evaluating long-lived assets for potential impairment, we first compare the carrying value of the asset&rsquo;s estimated future undiscounted cash flows.&nbsp; If the estimated future cash flows are less than the carrying value of the asset,
we calculate an impairment loss.&nbsp; The impairment loss calculation compares the carrying value of the asset to the assets estimated fair value.&nbsp; We recognize an impairment loss if the amount of the assets carrying value exceeds the assets estimated fair
value.&nbsp; If we recognize an impairment loss, the adjusted carrying amount of the asset becomes its new cost basis and, if applicable, will be depreciated over the remaining useful life of that asset.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Long-Lived Assets<br />
 </font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Our impairment loss calculations contain uncertainties as they require management to make assumptions and to apply judgment to estimate future cash flows and asset fair values.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><i><font size="2" face="Arial">Long-Lived Assets<br />
 </font></i></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">We have consistently applied our impairment loss methodology.&nbsp;&nbsp; As a result of our impairment tests in 2009 we recorded impairment charges of $1.3 million to write the long-lived assets to their estimated fair values.&nbsp;
The assets impaired were determined to have no value so no portion of the impairment charge will result in future cash expenditures.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Income Taxes<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">We record a valuation allowance against our deferred tax assets when we conclude it is more likely than not that we will be unable to generate adequate taxable income of the appropriate character, to utilize such assets.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Income Taxes<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">This determination requires management to make judgments regarding expectations of future taxable income.&nbsp; The Section 382 limitation may impact payments due or refundable under the tax agreement with Continental because the
certain deductions that are limited under Section 382 are the same tax attributes that drive our payment obligations under the tax agreement.</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">Income Taxes<br />
 </font></b></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">In 2009 we determined that is was more likely than not that we would not be able to realize approximately $280 million of our gross deferred tax assets.&nbsp; Consequently, we adjusted those assets to their net realizable values as of
December 31, 2009.&nbsp; The offset was recorded as a reduction to the valuation allowance of our deferred tax assets and liabilities.&nbsp; In addition, we also adjusted the valuation allowance by $17.1 million relating to a carryback claim with the Internal Revenue
Service that we expect to receive in 2010.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In addition to our critical accounting estimates and policies described above, we made other estimates that, while not involving the same degree of judgment, are
important to understanding our financial statements.&nbsp; In general, we base our estimates on historical experience, information from third-party professionals and various other assumptions that we believe are reasonable under the circumstances.&nbsp; We
continually evaluate our accounting policies and the estimates used to prepare our Consolidated Financial Statements.&nbsp; Our estimates as of the date of the financial statements reflect our best judgment after giving consideration to all currently available facts
and circumstances.&nbsp; As such, actual results may differ significantly from these estimates and may require adjustment in the future as additional facts become known or as circumstances change.</font></p>

<p><a name="ops2"></a><b><u><font size="2" face="Arial">Operations Review</font></u></b></p>

<p><u><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></u></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Under the terms of the Amended Continental CPA, we are not reimbursed for certain costs, primarily fuel, aircraft rent and certain ground handling services, which were
previously recorded as revenue.&nbsp; Accordingly revenues from July 1, 2008 forward under our contract flying with Continental are different than prior to the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; Additionally in September 2008, we ceased our Branded Flying which began in
April 2007.&nbsp; Accordingly, results between 2008 and 2007 are not comparable.</font></p>

<tr>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(1)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Revenue passenger miles are the number of scheduled miles flown by revenue passengers.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(2)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Available seat miles are the number of passenger seats available multiplied by the number of scheduled miles those seats are flown.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(3)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Passenger load factor equals revenue passenger miles divided by available seat miles.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(4)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Operating cost per available seat mile is operating costs divided by available seat miles.&nbsp; The reimbursable expenses are different under the terms of the Amended Continental CPA versus the Original Continental CPA, and therefore
costs are inconsistent with prior periods, beginning July 2008.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(5)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Block hours are the hours from gate departure to gate arrival.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(6)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Operating cost per block hour is operating costs divided by block hours.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(7)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Beginning in 2007, our fuel activity includes purchases to support our various business platforms outside of the Amended Continental CPA.&nbsp; These purchases were executed through agreements with independent third parties.&nbsp; Under
the Amended Continental CPA, Continental is directly responsible for the cost of providing fuel for all flights operating as Continental Express; therefore, the related fuel expense is no longer included in our Consolidated Statements of Operations for periods
subsequent to July 1, 2008.&nbsp; Prior to July 1, 2008 under our fuel purchase agreement with Continental, fuel and fuel tax expense were reconciled to the lower of the actual costs or the agreed-upon caps.&nbsp; From 2003 through July 1, 2008, our caps on fuel and
fuel taxes, for aircraft operating under the Original Continental CPA, were 66.0 cents and 5.2 cents per gallon, respectively.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td valign="top"></td>
<td valign="top">
<p align="right"><font size="2" face="Arial">(8)&nbsp;</font></p>
</td>
<td valign="top">
<p><font size="2" face="Arial">Average daily utilization of each aircraft is the average number of block hours per day that an aircraft is operated.</font></p>
</td>
</tr>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <b><i><u>Comparison of 2009 to 2008</u></i></b></font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></p>

<p><b><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Operating Revenue and Segment Profit / (Loss)</font></b></p>

<p><i><font size="2" face="Arial"></font></i></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Arial">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The table below (in millions, except percentage data) sets forth the changes in revenue, direct segment costs and segment profit from 2009 to 2008.&nbsp; A significant
portion of our operating expenses and infrastructure is integrated across segments (e.g., for non-airport facility rentals, outside services, general and administrative expenses) in order to support our entire fleet of 244 aircraft; therefore, we do not allocate
these costs to the individual segments identified above, but evaluate them for our consolidated operation.&nbsp; We believe that the presentation of our consolidated shared costs and transition costs is consistent with the manner in which these expenses are reviewed
by our chief operating decision makers.&nbsp; However, we continue to monitor the shared costs to identify direct segment expenses.&nbsp; For example, in 2009 our entire fleet of 244 aircraft operated within the Contract Flying segment.&nbsp; As such, aircraft
related expenses are now identified as direct segment costs within our Contract Flying segment.&nbsp; These costs are included as a part of the analysis of our operating expenses below.&nbsp;</font></p>
